frames.narration: The stack is declared in git: 1 network, 2 app servers (small) and 1 database (postgres15). Nothing exists yet, so the plan is: 4 to create.
Apply takes the state lock, creates the network first (the servers need it), then the servers and database, and records each real id in the state file.
A pull request changes both servers from small to medium. The plan is attached for review: 2 to update in place, 0 to replace. Reviewers approve a diff of the infrastructure, not just of the code.
After merge, apply resizes both servers in place. Planning again finds nothing to do: 0 changes. That is idempotence, and it makes re-running a failed apply safe.
During an incident someone resizes web-1 to large in the console. The code still says medium and nobody was told: that is drift.
The next plan refreshes from the real world, sees large against medium and proposes 1 update to revert it. Either apply (revert) or change the code to large (adopt it).

An upgrade changes the database engine from postgres15 to postgres16. That attribute is immutable, so the plan says: 1 to replace, forces replacement. Destroy then create means an empty database unless you restore a backup.
Renaming web-2 to app-2 in code looks harmless, but the state file knows only web-2. The plan is 1 destroy and 1 create. A move step tells the tool they are the same server.
A colleague runs apply at the same moment. The state lock is held, so the second run waits or fails instead of both writing the same state and corrupting it.
